rating.title: Customer reviews
rating.empty: Your first review arrives when a guest finishes their visit.
rating.effect: Reviews change arrivals only, never prices, tips or payment per order. Four stars means normal traffic; the effect ranges from −25% to +25%.
rating.smoothing: The first 20 reviews are smoothed toward four stars so one bad visit has limited impact. After that, the latest 50 count; better service replaces old reviews.
rating.rules: Taste sets the base: standard 4.0, practiced 4.5, signature 5.0. Combos average the dishes actually delivered. The final score is the lower of taste and the service cap, rounded to one decimal. In game time from arrival to handoff, the cap is 5/4/3 stars within 12/25/40 seconds, or 2 for longer waits. A missing add-on caps the score at 3. A sold-out main, table walkout or cancelled accepted order earns 1; a queue walkout earns 2.
rating.fairness: Each guest reviews once. People turned away by a full queue and queued guests sent home at closing leave no review.
rating.noReviews: No new reviews this session. Your reputation is unchanged.

promo.intro: Hire a creator on Douyin (豆音) or Xiaohongshu for a video or café feature. One campaign at a time; stock up and prepare your team first.
promo.platform.flash.desc: Café videos · A short burst of attention
promo.risk: More traffic does not guarantee sales or profit. Long queues, slow service and stockouts can earn bad reviews; promotion never directly lowers ratings. Capacity estimates exclude delivery, seating and stock bottlenecks.
promo.rules: The full fee is paid when booked. Closed-shop bookings begin when you open. Only active open game time is consumed, following the speed setting. Pausing, closing service and offline time consume nothing; unused time carries over. Pause and resume the same booking; no refunds, stacking or automatic renewal. Reports expense only airtime delivered that day, without charging cash again. Traffic multiplies with reputation, cats and other effects.

guide.title: First café guide
guide.stock.title: Check your starter stock
guide.stock.body: Your 50 starter beans are free. Each espresso uses 1 bean. Check the pantry first; no purchase is needed yet.
guide.prepare.title: Choose today’s menu
guide.prepare.body: Beans are ready. Keep espresso on the menu, then confirm Start business. Nothing opens until you choose.
guide.observe.title: Watch a few orders
guide.observe.body: Staff serve automatically; tapping is optional. Watch orders reach guests. Switching tabs pauses the café.
guide.close.title: Try closing your first day
guide.close.body: You can close whenever you like. No timer ends the day. Close now to finish accepted orders and see your results.
guide.closing.title: Finish accepted orders
guide.closing.body: New arrivals have stopped. Let staff finish; settlement opens automatically. “Settle now” discards unfinished work.
guide.reopen.title: Stock up and open again
guide.reopen.body: Check tomorrow’s stock in Prepare menu. Buy only what is missing; leftover ingredients keep. Your goal reward is in the panel.
guide.complete.title: Your café loop is ready
guide.complete.body: You stocked, served, settled and reopened. Explore the other tools when ready. This guide stays in Settings.
guide.helpTitle: Your café, one step at a time
guide.reference.stock.title: 1. Ingredients
guide.reference.stock.body: The pantry holds raw ingredients. Starter beans are free; later purchases reduce your cash. Stock for ~3 minutes buys a forecast, not an unlimited supply. Unused ingredients carry over.
guide.reference.menu.title: 2. Today’s menu
guide.reference.menu.body: Checked dishes are offered today. Unlocking a recipe does not supply its ingredients. Drinks are made to order; leave dishes without supplies off the menu while closed.
guide.reference.bake.title: Later: baking
guide.reference.bake.body: After building a kitchen, bake amounts mean portions made at opening. The kitchen replenishes during service. Too few can sell out; unsold shelf food goes stale at closing. Start with the suggested batch.
guide.reference.open.title: 3. Open and observe
guide.reference.open.body: Confirm Start business to open. Staff work automatically. Service status explains shortages and waiting. The café pauses in another tab, while closed, and during dialogs; it earns nothing in the background.
guide.reference.close.title: 4. Close and settle
guide.reference.close.body: The forecast is not a day timer. Close whenever you choose. New guests stop arriving while staff finish accepted orders. Settle now discards unfinished work, including ingredients already used.
guide.reference.next.title: 5. Prepare the next day
guide.reference.next.body: Profit is revenue minus consumed ingredients and running costs, not your cash balance. Read the next-step advice, claim ready goal rewards, reserve ingredient money, then prepare and open again. Kitchen, expansions, cats and promotion can wait.

regular.guest.mina.name: Mina
regular.guest.mina.personality: Careful and curious; rehearses her first sentence, then asks wonderful questions.
regular.guest.mina.chapter1.title: The First Index Card
regular.guest.mina.chapter1.text: My class is mapping the walk from the station to school, and I've filled six cards with facts but none with a first sentence. I came here to practise saying it aloud; so far, the sugar jar is a very patient audience.
regular.guest.mina.chapter2.title: Twenty Seconds
regular.guest.mina.chapter2.text: I managed a twenty-second recording of my opening, although the bus outside got the last word. Listening back, I realised I was listing street names without saying why anyone would take that walk. Tomorrow I'll try it with my notebook shut.
regular.guest.mina.chapter3.title: The Other Entrance
regular.guest.mina.chapter3.text: A classmate tested my route and found that I'd drawn the station stairs but missed the ramp around the side. We walked it together, and I added the crossing with the longer green light too. There's a lot you can't spot while staring at a neat little map.
regular.guest.mina.chapter4.title: A Ring on the Corner
regular.guest.mina.chapter4.text: I gave the presentation with a coffee ring on the corner of my last card. When someone asked about the ramp, I answered without looking down once. I've clipped that stained card to the finished map; it earned its place.
regular.guest.mina.chapter5.title: Room for a Pencil
regular.guest.mina.chapter5.text: Our map is up on the class noticeboard with a pencil tied beside it for corrections. Someone has already marked a bench I didn't know about, so I have a new stop to investigate. May I leave a copy here too, with plenty of room in the margins?

regular.guest.theo.name: Theo
regular.guest.theo.personality: Punctual and dryly funny; notices the details his timetable leaves out.
regular.guest.theo.chapter1.title: Seven Forty-Two
regular.guest.theo.chapter1.text: Train at 7:42, second carriage, same door: that's my weekday in three facts. The station coffee machine swallowed my coins this morning, so your café is an unscheduled entry. For the record, the chair is considerably better than platform two.
regular.guest.theo.chapter2.title: A Pencil Correction
regular.guest.theo.chapter2.text: The escalator is being repaired, and my usual shortcut now ends at a very definite fence. I tried the riverside entrance instead and still made my train. I've pencilled it into my timetable; apparently the timetable doesn't contain every useful fact.
regular.guest.theo.chapter3.title: The Longer Route
regular.guest.theo.chapter3.text: I timed the river route properly: four extra minutes, one heron, no traffic lights. The escalator is working again, but I went the long way anyway. I've decided not to put the heron in the spreadsheet; it would spoil the formatting.
regular.guest.theo.chapter4.title: Ten Minutes in Reserve
regular.guest.theo.chapter4.text: I left home ten minutes earlier today, then spent those ten minutes sitting here with my phone zipped away. No efficiency gains to report, unless finishing a warm drink counts. It felt suspiciously like getting part of the morning back.
regular.guest.theo.chapter5.title: The Blank Square
regular.guest.theo.chapter5.text: My new timetable has a blank square before the 7:42 train, labelled only 'here'. On rainy days that's this table; on clear days it's the bench by the river. Same train, same second carriage, slightly different weekday.
regular.guest.iris.name: Iris
regular.guest.iris.personality: Patient and practical; tells the weather by her pots and laughs at stubborn seedlings.
regular.guest.iris.chapter1.title: The Empty Tub
regular.guest.iris.chapter1.text: There's an old wooden tub in our courtyard that has spent two years growing nothing but lost pegs. I've cleared it, checked the drainage, and put in nasturtium seeds. The pegs have had a good run; it's the flowers' turn now.
regular.guest.iris.chapter2.title: Something Green
regular.guest.iris.chapter2.text: Two round little leaves have come up in the tub, looking as if someone left tiny umbrellas in the soil. I nearly watered them twice because I was so pleased, then checked with my finger and left the damp soil alone. Looking after something sometimes means putting the watering can down.
regular.guest.iris.chapter3.title: A Place to Lean
regular.guest.iris.chapter3.text: The stems have started reaching past the rim, so I made a low support from fallen twigs and soft string. The first version leaned worse than the plant did. Four crossed sticks later, everything is standing, including my pride.
regular.guest.iris.chapter4.title: After the Rain
regular.guest.iris.chapter4.text: Last night's rain loosened one tie, but the stem beneath it was fine. I retied the support and found the first tightly folded bud, hiding on the other side of the tub. Good thing repairs make you walk all the way around.
regular.guest.iris.chapter5.title: An Orange Visitor
regular.guest.iris.chapter5.text: The first flower opened this morning, bright orange against all those round leaves. A neighbour stopped to look and admitted one of the lost pegs was hers. I've left a little stool beside the tub now; apparently the courtyard has an attraction.
regular.guest.nico.name: Nico
regular.guest.nico.personality: Playful and observant; pockets odd shapes and learns to stop polishing every line.
regular.guest.nico.chapter1.title: A Street in My Pocket
regular.guest.nico.chapter1.text: I'm drawing a postcard of this street, small enough to post and large enough for every wonky drainpipe. I spent an hour making the café roof straight before noticing the real roof isn't. The building has better ideas about character than I do.
regular.guest.nico.chapter2.title: An Accidental Cat
regular.guest.nico.chapter2.text: A splash of wash landed in the postcard's empty corner, exactly where I had planned to put a very respectable tree. Two ears later, it was a cat sitting beside the drainpipe. The tree has been reassigned to the next drawing.
regular.guest.nico.chapter3.title: Only Two Inks
regular.guest.nico.chapter3.text: The print shop suggested two inks to keep my little postcard affordable, so the sky and the cat now share the same blue. I thought that would feel like losing a colour. Instead, the whole street looks as if it knows the same secret.
regular.guest.nico.chapter4.title: The Crooked Proof
regular.guest.nico.chapter4.text: The first proof came back with the blue layer a little off, giving every window a strange little shadow. We fixed the alignment for the final batch, but I kept the crooked one in my sketchbook. It's a useful reminder that charming and readable still need to get along.
regular.guest.nico.chapter5.title: Six on a String
regular.guest.nico.chapter5.text: June, who runs the bookshop, hung six postcards from a string by her till, and someone bought one before I'd finished explaining the blue cat. I used my own copy to write home instead of saving it in a drawer. Now this little street is going somewhere.
regular.guest.june.name: June
regular.guest.june.personality: Quietly witty and welcoming; remembers the book you meant even when you don't.
regular.guest.june.chapter1.title: The Squeaking Cart
regular.guest.june.chapter1.text: My bookshop cart announces every delivery with a squeak loud enough to count as a reading. I've decided to clear its bottom shelf for books people can borrow without buying. First I need somewhere else to put eleven years of spare paper bags.
regular.guest.june.chapter2.title: A Ticket in Chapter Four
regular.guest.june.chapter2.text: While sorting books for the cart, I found an old bus ticket between the pages of a gardening guide. Someone had underlined 'leave room to grow' twice. I've kept the ticket as its bookmark; whoever reads it next may appreciate the accidental advice.
regular.guest.june.chapter3.title: Help Yourself
regular.guest.june.chapter3.text: I wrote 'Please borrow a book' on the cart, but everyone kept asking whether I really meant it. A second sign now says 'Yes, really', which seems to have helped. The gardening guide went out before lunchtime.
regular.guest.june.chapter4.title: A Softer Wheel
regular.guest.june.chapter4.text: The cart is quiet at last: a loose wheel fitting needed tightening, not an elaborate farewell ceremony. The gardening guide came back too, with the bus ticket intact and a pencilled note recommending chapter six. I've put a little notebook on the shelf for more tips like that.
regular.guest.june.chapter5.title: A Good Empty Shelf
regular.guest.june.chapter5.text: Only two books were left on the borrowing shelf when I closed yesterday. For once, an empty patch in the shop means something is going well. I saved the last paper bag for returned books and recycled the rest; eleven years was quite enough.
regular.guest.alba.name: Alba
regular.guest.alba.personality: Warm and candid; turns small mishaps into invitations and slowly feels at home.
regular.guest.alba.chapter1.title: The Box Marked Kitchen
regular.guest.alba.chapter1.text: I've moved into the flat around the corner, and the box marked 'kitchen' contains three lamps and a scarf. All my mugs are somewhere else, probably enjoying a much better system. Until I find them, this may be my most organised breakfast spot.
regular.guest.alba.chapter2.title: One Curtain Too Short
regular.guest.alba.chapter2.text: I found the mugs inside the laundry basket, so that mystery is solved. The curtains are another matter: one stops a hand's width above the sill, and the evening sun goes straight through the gap. I've put my unpacking chair there; it turns out to be the nicest patch of light in the flat.
regular.guest.alba.chapter3.title: Four Different Bowls
regular.guest.alba.chapter3.text: I invited the people next door for noodles before counting my bowls; there are four, and none match. They brought their own chopsticks and said the funny curtain gap made the room look cheerful. We ate with the moving boxes still stacked behind us.
regular.guest.alba.chapter4.title: Letters by the Bell
regular.guest.alba.chapter4.text: My name is finally beside the doorbell, written on a strip cut from the last moving box. I put it in upside down the first time, which the neighbour from our noodle dinner spotted immediately. We agreed that's a better introduction than another anonymous bell.
regular.guest.alba.chapter5.title: A Place for the Spare Mug
regular.guest.alba.chapter5.text: The boxes are gone, but I've kept the short curtain and the four mismatched bowls. There's a spare mug by the kettle for whoever knocks, and I know which bell is mine without checking now. I'll still come here for breakfast; it's nice having more than one familiar doorway.
regular.guest.ren.name: Ren
regular.guest.ren.personality: Quick, good-humoured and alert; knows every shortcut but is learning where to stop.
regular.guest.ren.chapter1.title: One Extra Rattle
regular.guest.ren.chapter1.text: I can usually name a street by the rattle it gives my bicycle, but today the bike kept making the same noise everywhere. Turns out a loose lunch tin was bouncing in the front basket. I've come in to eat the evidence before my next delivery.
regular.guest.ren.chapter2.title: Number Twenty-Seven A
regular.guest.ren.chapter2.text: I spent ten minutes looking for 27A, which lives behind a gate labelled simply '27'. The resident showed me the side entrance and said every courier gets lost there. With their permission, I sketched the turn in the depot's route notebook; one mystery fewer for the next rider.
regular.guest.ren.chapter3.title: The Blue Circle
regular.guest.ren.chapter3.text: Someone added a blue circle to my route sketch: a public tap beside the little square. I've marked a bike rack and a sheltered bench too, in a different colour from the delivery stops. A useful route can have places where you aren't going anywhere.
regular.guest.ren.chapter4.title: Rain on the Map
regular.guest.ren.chapter4.text: Rain blurred the corner of the notebook, so I copied our notes onto a fresh sheet and slipped it into a clear sleeve. Another rider corrected the square's opening hours before I made copies. The map is slower work than a delivery, but it's getting more useful with every pair of eyes.
regular.guest.ren.chapter5.title: A Stop of My Own
regular.guest.ren.chapter5.text: The depot has copies of our little map now, and 27A even has a clearer sign. I've added one private mark to mine: this café, for a break after the last delivery. The lunch tin stays quiet these days; I actually empty it on time.
regular.guest.tess.name: Tess
regular.guest.tess.personality: Bright and resourceful; sees a place for bent stems and asks direct, cheerful questions.
regular.guest.tess.chapter1.title: The Crooked Stems
regular.guest.tess.chapter1.text: A delivery arrived at the flower shop with three perfectly healthy stems bent into the shape of question marks. They won't fit the tall bouquet I planned, but throwing them out would feel ridiculous. I've brought my sketchbook to work out what sort of vase likes questions.
regular.guest.tess.chapter2.title: Low and Wide
regular.guest.tess.chapter2.text: The answer was a low bowl, not a taller vase: the stems lean out over the edge as if they're chatting. My manager let me try the arrangement in the shop window. I turned the most crooked flower toward the street; it deserved the best view.
regular.guest.tess.chapter3.title: Just Because
regular.guest.tess.chapter3.text: Someone liked the window bowl but asked whether it was strange to buy flowers with no occasion. I wrote a tiny card saying 'Just because' and tucked it beside the display. By closing time, two people had asked for the same card with their flowers.
regular.guest.tess.chapter4.title: A Different Kind of Order
regular.guest.tess.chapter4.text: We got an order for a little kitchen table: nothing tall, nothing formal, and definitely room left for toast. I used the low-bowl idea with fresh stems and checked its width against a breakfast plate. That's the first arrangement I've designed around crumbs.
regular.guest.tess.chapter5.title: The Bent-Stem Notebook
regular.guest.tess.chapter5.text: I've started a notebook of small arrangements, with a photo of those three question-mark stems on the first page. My manager wants one new window idea each week, and I've already drawn a vase made from an old teapot. It has a spout, which feels like a very promising complication.
regular.guest.sam.name: Sam
regular.guest.sam.personality: Reserved and steady; prefers useful things and shows affection by making them work again.
regular.guest.sam.chapter1.title: A Tune That Stops
regular.guest.sam.chapter1.text: A customer brought in a wind-up music box that stops halfway through its tune. She doesn't remember the song's name, only that her father used to wind it after supper. I've put it on the quiet end of the bench; some jobs need listening space.
regular.guest.sam.chapter2.title: The Small Missing Piece
regular.guest.sam.chapter2.text: The music box has a damaged gear, and the maker stopped producing that size long ago. I found a possible match in my drawer of parts worth keeping, right under a button that has no business being there. I'll check the fit before promising anything.
regular.guest.sam.chapter3.title: Beyond the Pause
regular.guest.sam.chapter3.text: The replacement fits, and today the tune made it past the place where it always stopped. It still runs unevenly, so there's more adjusting to do. I caught myself holding my breath for that one extra note.
regular.guest.sam.chapter4.title: The Whole Song
regular.guest.sam.chapter4.text: I played the music box for its owner, and she hummed the ending before it reached it. She still couldn't name the song, but that didn't seem important anymore. We left the scratch on the lid alone; she said she'd made it herself years ago.
regular.guest.sam.chapter5.title: Space in the Drawer
regular.guest.sam.chapter5.text: The music box is home, and there's one useful gap in my spare-parts drawer. I finally sorted the drawer and put that stray button in its own tin. When I closed the shop, I was still humming a tune I don't know the name of.
regular.guest.vivi.name: Vivi
regular.guest.vivi.personality: Expressive and self-deprecating; talks in musical phrases and makes room for quieter voices.
regular.guest.vivi.chapter1.title: One Beat Early
regular.guest.vivi.chapter1.text: I joined the community choir and made a spectacular entrance, exactly one beat before everyone else. The conductor said enthusiasm was welcome, though preferably on the right beat. I've drawn a giant rest on my music, just in case enthusiasm can't read small print.
regular.guest.vivi.chapter2.title: The Pencil Mark
regular.guest.vivi.chapter2.text: The singer beside me showed me where to breathe, and suddenly the long phrase felt possible. I lent her my spare pencil because hers had worn down to a wooden whisper. We now have matching marks in our scores, which feels like a very quiet sort of teamwork.
regular.guest.vivi.chapter3.title: Without the Loudest Voice
regular.guest.vivi.chapter3.text: Our loudest singer was away, so rehearsal sounded alarmingly empty for the first few bars. Then I could hear a low harmony I'd never noticed, and I tried fitting my voice around it. We finished more softly than usual, but nobody had disappeared.
regular.guest.vivi.chapter4.title: The Hall Rehearsal
regular.guest.vivi.chapter4.text: We rehearsed in the little hall today, where every footstep sounds important and the last row is surprisingly far away. I missed a word, found the next line, and kept going with everyone else. The giant pencil rest did its job; my entrance was right on time.
regular.guest.vivi.chapter5.title: The Last Note
regular.guest.vivi.chapter5.text: The concert ended, and for one lovely second the last chord seemed to stay in the hall without us. Then someone in the back clapped too early, which I appreciated on a personal level. I've signed up for the next term and bought a whole box of pencils to share.
regular.guest.otto.name: Otto
regular.guest.otto.personality: Measured and kind; remembers doorways and takes the small responsibilities seriously.
regular.guest.otto.chapter1.title: The Unsent Postcard
regular.guest.otto.chapter1.text: I found a seaside postcard in an old coat pocket, bought for my sister last year and never posted. I deliver letters all day, yet apparently I can carry one around for twelve months without noticing. There's a gull printed in the corner, looking rather disappointed in me.
regular.guest.otto.chapter2.title: What I Remember
regular.guest.otto.chapter2.text: I tried writing about the trip and couldn't remember the hotel's name or the day we arrived. What I do remember is a pebble getting into my shoe while I ate a melting ice cream. I think my sister would rather hear about that than a perfect itinerary.
regular.guest.otto.chapter3.title: Through the Slot
regular.guest.otto.chapter3.text: The postcard is written: one stubborn pebble, one crooked gull, and a question about the shelf we built in her kitchen. I put a stamp on it and slipped it into the postbox after my round. For once, I don't know exactly which pair of hands will carry the next part.
regular.guest.otto.chapter4.title: The Crooked Shelf
regular.guest.otto.chapter4.text: My sister replied with a photo of the kitchen shelf, still slightly crooked and still holding her teacups. She remembers the day we built it because I dropped a screw into the flour tin. Her letter was mostly ordinary things; I read it twice before taking my coat off.
regular.guest.otto.chapter5.title: One Blank Card
regular.guest.otto.chapter5.text: I've put her letter in the drawer beside my stamps, and a fresh blank card in my bag. This time I'll write about the café window and the first yellow leaf on my round, before I forget them. My sister says the kitchen shelf has room for one more postcard.
regular.guest.luz.name: Luz
regular.guest.luz.personality: Thoughtful and gently playful; listens for what people mean and keeps room for their own words.
regular.guest.luz.chapter1.title: A Little, Enough
regular.guest.luz.chapter1.text: I'm translating my grandmother's recipe notebook for a cousin who lives abroad. Her measurements include 'a little', 'the blue bowl', and 'you'll know when it's enough'. I translate for a living, but the blue bowl may be my toughest reference yet.
regular.guest.luz.chapter2.title: The Bowl on the Shelf
regular.guest.luz.chapter2.text: I found the blue bowl on the top kitchen shelf, with a tiny chip near the rim that marks her usual water level. We measured it together and wrote the amount beside the old words. She insisted I keep 'the blue bowl' too, because otherwise it wouldn't sound like her.
regular.guest.luz.chapter3.title: What She Meant by Golden
regular.guest.luz.chapter3.text: We cooked the flatbreads together, and I discovered that her 'golden' means the colour underneath, not the flour-dusted top. I took a photo of one turned over and added it to the draft. Some words become much easier when you can lift the pan.
regular.guest.luz.chapter4.title: Both Pages
regular.guest.luz.chapter4.text: The booklet is laid out with her handwritten page on the left and my translation on the right. I was about to clean up a flour smudge in the scan, then noticed it covered a correction she'd made. We kept the smudge and added a note; the recipe had learned something there.
regular.guest.luz.chapter5.title: Two Kitchens
regular.guest.luz.chapter5.text: My cousin sent a photo of the finished flatbreads, along with a note about the different flour she used. Grandmother wants that note on the next page, in both languages. The booklet finally has a title: 'The Blue Bowl', which now belongs in two kitchens.
